children.text: Caleruega Church is the Transfiguration Chapel inside a retreat center that the Dominican Order built on a hill in Batulao, Nasugbu, in 1994. Its red-brick exterior, the stained glass behind the altar and the garden paths make it an easy add-on to a day trip to Tagaytay.

Caleruega Church is formally called the Transfiguration Chapel. It stands in Barangay Kaylaway, Nasugbu, Batangas, on the hilly area commonly called Batulao. It is often bundled with Tagaytay trips because it is only about
30 minutes
farther west from central Tagaytay, but administratively it belongs to Nasugbu in Batangas, not to Cavite. Knowing this avoids confusion on map apps.

The chapel is part of the Caleruega retreat center, which the Dominican Order created in 1994 for retreats and seminars. The name comes from Caleruega, the town in Castile, Spain, where St. Dominic, the founder of the Dominicans, was born. The grounds cover about
8 hectares

and are owned by the Dominicans, and the complex is said to have been designed jointly by architect Yolanda Reyes and Dominican priest Fr. Ed Nantes. The mix of Spanish, Moorish and Filipino styles and the pine-planted hill have been compared to a Mediterranean village.

The Transfiguration Chapel is a red-brick building at the very top of the hill. It has a round arched entrance and a circular rose window, and a sloping wooden ceiling covers the interior. Behind the altar are stained-glass windows telling Bible stories, including the Transfiguration of Jesus, and the light is most beautiful on a clear afternoon. Sources give its capacity as anywhere from about 150 to 200 people, which is why it is so popular for small weddings.

There is far more here than just the chapel. A garden path follows the slope of the hill, and koi ponds, small gardens, a suspension bridge, a tent chapel and an outdoor theater are scattered around the grounds. A lookout partway along the path gives views of the Mount Batulao ridge. Remember that this is a place of prayer before it is a tourist spot, and that some areas may be closed on days with weddings or retreats. Sources differ, but 2–4 hours is usually enough to walk around the whole site.

This red-brick chapel sits at the top of the hill. The round arched entrance and circular rose window stand out, and the stained glass behind the altar shows Bible scenes including the Transfiguration. The door is sometimes locked, so please check on site.
The path from the parking area up to the chapel has about

steps, known as the Dominican Steps. The slope is fairly steep, so hold the handrail and climb slowly. You can catch your breath at the midway lookout while gazing at Mount Batulao. The view of the grounds and hills from the top of the stairway is the site's classic photo scene.
The path along the hillside is said to symbolize the journey of life. It links St. Dominic Point, Rosary Lane and benches with 180-degree views, and plenty of shade makes it easy to walk.
Small koi ponds and pocket gardens are scattered around, and crossing the suspension bridge leads to the tent chapel. It is where visiting families take the most photos with their children.

The facade shows St. Dominic, the coats of arms of both families, and sculptures of Thomas Aquinas and Catherine of Siena. The star and sun motifs associated with St. Dominic repeat on fountains, windows and lattices, so spotting them is part of the fun. A metal sculpture by Benhur Villanueva is also said to stand in front of the chapel.

This small chapel was made from an old convent building near the parking area. It is relatively quiet even on busy event days and is good for a short prayer. Before the statue of Our Lady on the grounds, worshippers can be seen touching the hem of her robe as they pray.

The grounds have a large function hall, a dining hall, dormitories, cottages and a campsite, used for weddings, seminars and family retreats. Weddings may be scheduled on weekends, so it is best to check before you go.

items.title: Half Day with Tagaytay
items.subtitle: Arrive in the morning for the gardens and the chapel

children.text: Leave central Tagaytay and take the highway toward Nasugbu. After the Nasugbu welcome arch, turn left at the KC Hillcrest (formerly Evercrest) entrance and turn right at the Caleruega sign.
Arrive at the parking area, pay the entrance fee and look around the grounds. Early in the morning the sun is gentle and there are fewer wedding photo crews.
Climb the Dominican Steps to the Transfiguration Chapel. View the altar and the stained glass quietly, and stay a moment if you wish to pray.
Walk down the garden path past the koi pond, the suspension bridge, the tent chapel and Rosary Lane.
Head back to Tagaytay for lunch, or continue to People's Park in the Sky and other Tagaytay viewpoints.
If you include this in a full-day plan, combining it with a Mount Batulao hike or Nasugbu beaches on the same day makes the schedule tight. This route takes only 2–4 hours.
Leave Manila by private car or rental car and take the South Luzon Expressway to the Sta. Rosa exit.
Pass through Tagaytay and drive toward Nasugbu to reach Caleruega. Traffic builds up in Tagaytay on weekends, so leave early.
Finish the chapel and the gardens and head back toward Tagaytay.
Have lunch in Tagaytay and stop at one or two viewpoints.
Leave for Manila before sunset. Sunday evening is crowded with returning traffic, so allow extra time.

items.title: From Manila by Car or Rental

children.text: From Manila, take the South Luzon Expressway (SLEX) to the Sta. Rosa exit and head up to Tagaytay. From Tagaytay, follow the highway west toward Nasugbu.
After the Nasugbu welcome arch, turn left at the KC Hillcrest entrance and turn right when you see the Caleruega sign.
There is also a route via the coastal road. Nasugbu is about
95 km
from Manila, which takes a little over 2 hours when traffic is good.
Some reviews say that Google Maps does not guide the last stretch accurately. Check road signs together with your map app.
Take a bus bound for Nasugbu, Balayan or Calatagan from a bus terminal along EDSA in Pasay. Check the operating companies and fares at the terminal on the day of your visit.
Tell the driver to drop you at the Evercrest (now KC Hillcrest) or Batulao stop.
From where you get off, a tricycle takes you to Caleruega. Agree on the round-trip fare and the return time beforehand.
From central Tagaytay, take a bus or jeepney toward Nasugbu and get off near Batulao.
When taxis or Grab are available, going straight to Caleruega is the easiest option. A ride back may not be available, so agree on a waiting fee with the driver in advance.
Many reviews say the last stretch of road is narrow and rough. Take extra care after rain.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) it takes about
2–3 hours
by car to Tagaytay, and a little longer to Caleruega in Nasugbu. It varies greatly with traffic.
In the dry season,
November–May
, skies are clear and you can see the stained glass and the Batulao ridge at their sharpest. The hill is high, so it is cool like Tagaytay, and a morning stroll is comfortable.
However, in the peak wedding months of December and January, and on weekends, the chapel and gardens can be crowded with weddings and photo crews. Weekday mornings are the quietest.

The grounds have dormitories, cottages and a campsite, but they are mainly for retreats and group events. Individual travelers may find it hard to stay overnight, so if you need lodging, contact them first. Contact details and the latest news are available on their Facebook page, CaleruegaPhilippines.

Most people eat in Tagaytay or central Nasugbu. Tagaytay has many restaurants with views, and the Alfonso, Cavite side has garden restaurants. There is also a large dining hall on the grounds, but it is for events and you cannot tell whether it is open to the public, so it is safer to bring your own water and snacks.

The facilities on the grounds have their own names. There is Veritas Hall for weddings and meetings, Gazekubo, a small meeting room, the large Refectory Hall for meals, men's and women's dormitories, cabin-style rooms and a campsite. All are mainly for groups, so it is best to inquire by phone or email before visiting about lodging or events. These facility names are written slightly differently in reviews and official notices, so check the signs on site as well.
Opening hours differ slightly between sources, but are usually given as
to
. Check the latest hours on the day of your visit.
There are many garden and stair sections, so bring comfortable sneakers, water, a hat and sunscreen.
Plan for about
2–4 hours
. If you see only the chapel, 1–2 hours is enough.
Sunday Mass times may change. If you plan to attend Mass, check on the Facebook page.
No dress code is posted, but because it is a Catholic chapel, modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees is appropriate.
Remove your hat inside the chapel and silence your phone. Do not take photos close to people who are praying.
Bring cash. It is used for the entrance fee, parking and tricycle fares.
Arrange your ride back in advance. It is a remote road and taxis may be hard to find.
The most comfortable order is to see the chapel in the morning and rest in Tagaytay in the afternoon. The sun is strong around noon.
If photography is your goal, the light is softest in the morning around 9–10 AM or around 4 PM, when the sun is low. The stained glass colors are most vivid at midday on a clear day.
The chapel or some areas may be closed depending on weddings and retreat schedules. Check the latest announcements before you visit.
The whole site is not easy for wheelchairs or strollers. There are steps, slopes, outdoor paths and a suspension bridge.
After rain, the steps and dirt paths are slippery. Wear shoes with a firm sole.
Do not take photos close to a bride and groom during a shoot or enter reception areas. Drones and large lights may need prior permission.
The entrance fee and opening hours differ by source and may change on site. Bring plenty of cash and check the latest announcements.
On weekend and holiday afternoons the road through Tagaytay is congested. A plan to go early and leave early works best.
This highland city is about
30 minutes
away by car. With views of Taal Lake and a dining district, it pairs well with a Caleruega visit on the same day.
A popular hiking mountain whose ridge is visible even from the lookout in front of the chapel. It is safer to plan the hike separately, at dawn.
A hilltop park east of Tagaytay with good views. It is a good stop on the way back from Caleruega to Tagaytay.
A garden restaurant in Alfonso, Cavite. It is often mentioned as a lunch stop on the way back from Caleruega toward Tagaytay.
